question: How can an agent learn value functions online by combining Monte Carlo sampling with dynamic-programming bootstrapping, and how do Q-learning, SARSA, n-step methods and eligibility traces differ in practice?
contributions: Derives TD learning from MC and DP updates (Eq 3-1 to 3-4)
Presents Q-learning (off-policy) and SARSA (on-policy) with pseudocode (Algorithms 3-1, 3-2)
Compares them on a cliff gridworld and on real-time-bidding environments built from the iPinYou data

Covers double, delayed and opposition-based Q-learning, n-step SARSA (Algorithm 3-3) and SARSA(lambda) with eligibility traces (Algorithm 3-4), plus Watkins's Q(lambda), fuzzy wipes, speedy Q-learning and accumulating vs replacing traces

results.claim: In the cliff gridworld SARSA tends to earn higher and less noisy reward than Q-learning, because it learns the safe path far from the cliff while Q-learning hugs the edge and sometimes falls.
results.setup: Gridworld with a cliff along one edge: -1 per step, -100 for falling off, 0 at goal; cliff and goal terminal; tabular agents with epsilon-greedy exploration (epsilon, alpha, gamma values for Fig 3-2 are lost in the extracted text); average sum of rewards per episode over 100 parallel experiments, 500 episodes
results.quote: in which the plots show the average sum of rewards over 100 parallel experiments.

results.claim: Early in training the reward dips below the random agent's start: episode reward falls to roughly -125 after a few episodes because the agent steers away from the cliff, wastes -1 steps, then falls anyway.

results.claim: n-step SARSA with n = 2 and n = 4 learns optimal trajectories faster than 1-step SARSA on the grid, at the cost of extra computation and memory.

results.claim: Double Q-learning gives a better policy than standard Q-learning on the grid; delayed Q-learning ends with a very good result but with worrying discontinuities and stops learning after a fixed number of updates.

limits: Experiments are single small tabular environments (cliff grid, a toy RTB environment, one real-data RTB set) with no hyperparameter values, seeds or error bars in the text; Fig 3-2 settings are in symbols lost from the text layer.
Tabular methods only: cannot handle continuous states or actions (author defers to chapters 4 and 5).
The RTB agent is trained on a limited amount of data so training takes seconds instead of hours, with a deliberately bad initial bid; reward is impression count, not clicks.
Author's own rule-of-thumb claims (lambda < 1, 'eligibility traces perform better than Q-learning in most cases') are asserted, not shown with numbers.
Written in 2020: the 'recent research' and 'only recently exploited' off-policy remarks predate DQN-era and LLM RL practice.
Chapter says importance sampling is not used in its off-policy versions and defers it to a later chapter.
practices: Prefer Q-learning when the greedy value matters and exploration noise is harmless; prefer SARSA when exploration mistakes are costly (cliff example, p. 10-11).
Treat n in n-step methods as a tuned hyperparameter; larger n costs computation and memory (p. 24).
For nontrivial tasks use lambda > 0 but keep it below 1 (p. 28).
Most practical effort goes to the state representation and reward definition, not the algorithm; tabular methods require simplified, small state spaces (p. 15, 17-18).
Spread an RTB budget across a batch by putting average affordable bid in the state; add constraints such as error clipping for stability (p. 15, 17).
Use a model only if it truly represents system dynamics; otherwise it biases the policy (p. 13).

terms.definition: updating an estimate from another estimate (the discounted prediction of the next state) rather than waiting for a full-episode return
a combination of these two approaches [MC and DP]: learns directly from experience by sampling, but also bootstraps
off-policy TD control that uses argmax over next-state actions in the TD error
on-policy TD control whose delta uses the next action actually chosen by the policy
stores an expected-value estimate for each state-action pair in a table, so cannot handle continuous states or actions
a tracer value per state-action pair that marks it as eligible for later updates and decays exponentially
expected return that uses n real rewards then the value estimate n steps ahead
